title: Record where an applied package came from
description:
The repository's applied-profile record carries the location the package was read from, so a later run can read the same package again.

## Background

The record beside an applied profile carries its id, its version, its origin, the package's content address, and a digest per installed target. Origin has one value, meaning the bytes were compiled into the binary — a vocabulary shaped for a second one but never given it. So a repository that applied a package from a directory has nowhere to say so, and nothing that runs later has anywhere to look for the bytes.

The location belongs in this record and nowhere else. It is repository-local state, versioned with the repository that applied the profile, and it is the one place that has to agree with itself. Putting the same location in a configuration key as well would create two carriers of one fact and a precedence question between them.

Where the location may point is part of the contract. A location outside the worktree makes a repository's derived-state repair depend on machine state, so the record is confined to a worktree-relative path and an application from outside it is refused rather than recorded.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The applied-profile record carries the repository-relative location the package was read from.
- [hard] REQ-02: The recorded location lies inside the repository worktree; applying a package from outside it is refused, naming the path.
- [hard] REQ-03: The record's origin distinguishes a package read from a repository location from one compiled into the binary.
- [hard] REQ-04: Application records the location it actually read from, not one supplied independently of the bytes.
- [hard] REQ-05: A record whose location is absent or malformed is a validation failure rather than an ignored field.

## Notes

The record carries a path, never package content. No package bytes are written under the tracker's data root.

planning.outcome: The applied-profile record carries the worktree-relative location the package was read from, and its origin.

terminal.test_boundary: in-crate application assertions over the written record
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One field on a persisted record and one variant on its origin, written where application already builds it.

title: Resolve a profile package from a given location or the repository's record
description:
The profile commands read their package from a location the caller gives or from the location the repository's own record names, so a package that is not compiled in can be inspected, applied, and re-read.

## Background

Resolution today compares a requested id against one compiled-in package and returns it or reports the profile missing, and enumeration returns a one-element list built from that same package. Neither can express a package that lives in a directory, so every profile command is limited to the one the binary carries.

Two routes replace it, in a fixed order. A location the caller gives answers the first application: an adopter who has obtained a package has bytes and no record yet. The location the repository's record names answers every run after that, without the caller having to remember where the package came from. While a package is still compiled in, it stays as the last resort behind both, so nothing that works today stops working before the package it depends on has left.

Enumeration follows the same principle: what the repository reports is what its own records name, each resolved from its recorded location, so the answer describes this repository rather than the binary.

A recorded location that no longer resolves is a failure and says so. Reporting it as an absent profile would make a deleted directory look like a repository that never applied one.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A profile command reads its package from an explicitly given repository location when one is supplied.
- [hard] REQ-02: With no location supplied, a profile command reads the package from the location the repository's applied-profile record names.
- [hard] REQ-03: A supplied location takes precedence over a recorded one, and both take precedence over any package compiled into the binary.
- [hard] REQ-04: Enumeration reports the profiles the repository's own records name, each resolved from its recorded location.
- [hard] REQ-05: A recorded location that no longer resolves is reported as an error naming the record and the path, never as an absent profile.
- [hard] REQ-06: The adopter-facing command reference describes the supplied-location form on every command that accepts it.

## Notes

Initialization applying a profile takes the same supplied location, because a repository being created has no record to read.

planning.outcome: The profile commands read a package from a given location or from the location the repository's record names.

terminal.test_boundary: command-harness assertions over the profile commands
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One resolver and one enumerator replace a compiled-in comparison and a literal list, behind flags the commands already parse.

title: Repair profile-owned targets from the recorded package location
description:
Derived-state repair recomputes a recorded profile's expected targets by reading its package again from the location the record names, and fails loudly when that location no longer resolves.

## Background

Repair works today because the package is always obtainable: the expected record can be recomputed from it and compared against the stored one, and only an exact match yields the claims that restore a deleted or edited profile-owned target. Once the package lives in a directory, "the package is resolvable" and "the binary exists" stop being the same statement, and repair needs somewhere to look.

The record's own location is that place, and it is the only one. The alternative — trusting the stored digests when the package cannot be read — would quietly turn repair from restoring profile-owned targets into restoring the ones it can still account for, which is a regression in the coherence the repair path exists to uphold.

So an unresolvable location is an error that names the record and the path. A repository with no applied-profile record is untouched: it resolves no package and reports nothing about profiles, which is already true and stays true.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Where a record names a location that resolves, repair recomputes the expected record from the package read there and restores a deleted or edited profile-owned target.
- [hard] REQ-02: Where the recorded location does not resolve, validation fails naming the record and the path.
- [hard] REQ-03: No expected target is ever derived from the stored record's own digests.
- [hard] REQ-04: A repository with no applied-profile record reads no package and reports nothing about profiles.
- [hard] REQ-05: A stored record that disagrees with the package read from the recorded location is a validation failure rather than a repair.

## Notes

This is what keeps the repair guarantee whole once the bytes leave the binary; the location's confinement to the worktree is what keeps it a property of the repository rather than of the machine.

planning.outcome: Repair recomputes a recorded profile's expected targets by re-reading its package from the recorded location.

terminal.test_boundary: the derived-state repair suite
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One resolution step inside the repair plan that already captures and compares profile targets.

title: A profile package is read from disk rather than from the binary
description:
The engine reads, verifies, applies, and repairs a profile package that lives in a repository directory, so a profile no longer has to be compiled in to exist.

## Background

A profile can presently exist only as bytes compiled into the binary: one constructor walks a compiled-in directory, one resolver compares a requested id against one compiled-in package, and the applied-profile record's origin has a single value meaning exactly that. Everything else about the package model already treats its bytes as untrusted external data.

What is missing is a reader, somewhere to record where a package came from, and a resolver that uses it. Together they make a package on disk a first-class one, and they leave repair working: the record names the location, and repair reads the package there rather than trusting what it stored.

One thing deliberately stays missing. A package declares which jit versions it is written for, and that declaration is parsed and not matched against the running binary; a package built for a later binary applies cleanly and fails wherever the shape later differs. Matching it belongs to the profile lifecycle the charter defers (`@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-19`).

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A profile package is constructed from a repository directory, with every existing package defence applying to it.
- [hard] REQ-02: The applied-profile record carries the worktree-relative location the package was read from.
- [hard] REQ-03: Profile inspection, application, and initialization read their package from a given location or from the recorded one.
- [hard] REQ-04: Derived-state repair recomputes expected targets from the package read at the recorded location, and fails loudly when it cannot.

## Notes

Nothing here removes the compiled-in package; it becomes the last resort behind two better answers, and leaves when the work that puts the package in the release archive has landed.

planning.outcome: The engine reads, verifies, applies, and repairs a profile package that lives in a repository directory.

title: Move the coverage-preview rule transform out of the bracket module
description:
The pure rule transform that derives a preview coverage rule sits with the engine's rule constructors, so it does not depend on a module that is about to be removed.

## Background

The transform takes a closure coverage rule and a breakdown type name and returns the preview form of that rule, with the child-state condition omitted so drafted children count at plan time. It is parameterized by the type name its caller supplies, names no workflow type of its own, and its own tests exercise a type name that is not this repository's. By the criterion separating engine capability from a specific application, it is engine capability.

It lives in a module whose other contents are one workflow's gate presets, and that module is being emptied. Leaving the transform there would leave engine capability inside a module named for the workflow that left, which is the shape the cutover rule exists to prevent; removing it with the presets would delete capability that the criterion keeps.

Moving it first means the removal that follows takes only what the criterion excludes.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The transform that derives a preview coverage rule from a closure rule lives with the engine's rule declarations.
- [hard] REQ-02: It stays parameterized by the breakdown type its caller supplies, and names no workflow type of its own.
- [hard] REQ-03: Its tests move with it and still exercise a type name that is not this repository's.
- [hard] REQ-04: No module named for the planning bracket exports it, and its published path is the new one.

## Notes

The move is a relocation, not a rewrite: its behaviour, its signature, and the error it reports for a rule of the wrong shape are unchanged.

planning.outcome: The pure coverage-preview rule transform sits with the engine's rule constructors.

terminal.test_boundary: in-crate rule-construction assertions
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One function and its tests move between modules, with no change to what either asserts.

title: Resolve this repository's own package from its checkout
description:
This repository's own tests and scaffolding obtain its profile package by assembling it from the checkout, so none of them depends on the package being compiled in.

## Background

Several places here read the compiled-in package for reasons that have nothing to do with an adopter: the render that keeps this repository's template registry in agreement with the packaged declaration, the assertions over packaged asset content and modes, the initialization and profile command tests, the derived-state repair tests, and the provenance fixture that seeds an isolated repository. All of them want this repository's package; the embed is merely how they have been getting it.

Assembling it from the checkout is now the direct answer, and it is the only one that survives the package leaving the binary. One entry point resolves the checkout from the crate's own manifest directory, so it does not depend on which directory a test process runs in, and returns the assembled package.

The provenance fixture is the one caller whose reason disappears rather than moves. It carves packaged sources under the tracker's data root into the repository it seeds so that a build inside that repository could read them. No build reads them any more, so the carve-out goes rather than being retargeted.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: One test-support entry point returns this repository's profile package, assembled from its checkout.
- [hard] REQ-02: Every test and test-support caller that read the compiled-in package reads it through that entry point.
- [hard] REQ-03: The entry point resolves the checkout from the crate's own manifest directory, so it is independent of the process working directory.
- [hard] REQ-04: The provenance fixture no longer carves packaged sources into the repository it seeds, and its documentation states the inventory it seeds without them.

## Notes

This changes what those callers read, not what they assert; every existing assertion over the package holds afterwards.

planning.outcome: This repository's tests read its profile package from the assembly rather than from the compiled-in copy.

terminal.test_boundary: the crate's own suite over the located package
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One entry point replaces one call in each of a handful of callers, with every assertion unchanged.

title: Carry the assembled package in the release archive
description:
The release archive carries the assembled profile package beside the binaries, so an adopter who unpacks one download can apply the profile offline with no second fetch, and the release's own smoke path proves it.

## Background

A release publishes one GitHub release whose native archive is flat and carries four files: the two binaries and the two license texts. The profile has never been among them, because it has always travelled inside the binary. Once it does not, an adopter has to obtain it, and where it arrives decides what the install costs them.

It arrives in the same archive. A separate asset would mean a second download and a second checksum step before a repository can be initialized, which is what the profile reference's offline promise exists to avoid; putting the package directory beside the binaries keeps one download sufficient, adds no asset to the published set, and leaves the existing checksum covering it because it covers the archive. The on-disk form stays a directory, so whoever applies it points at the extracted path and the runtime needs no archive support of its own.

The smoke path is what makes the package more than a file in a tarball. It already extracts the archive into a clean prefix and initializes a repository through the profile quickstart; pointing that step at the extracted package proves the published bytes apply, and it proves it from the moment they are published rather than from the moment the compiled-in copy goes.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The native archive carries the assembled profile package directory beside the binaries and the license texts.
- [hard] REQ-02: The published asset set is unchanged — no asset is added — and the existing checksum file covers the archive that now carries the package.
- [hard] REQ-03: The archive-verification step asserts the package directory is present in the extracted prefix.
- [hard] REQ-04: The smoke path applies the profile from the extracted package rather than from the binary or from a checkout, and still observes an exact re-application reporting no work.
- [hard] REQ-05: The adopter-facing statements of what the archive carries account for the package directory.
- [hard] REQ-06: Any job the change introduces is declared in the workflow contract, so no undeclared workflow or job enters.

## Notes

The archive carries the package directories this repository ships; there is one today, and the mechanism established here is what a second one rides on.

This lands before the compiled-in package is removed, so no published release exists in which the profile is reachable only from a jit source checkout.

planning.outcome: The release archive carries the assembled profile package beside the binaries, and the smoke path applies the profile from it.

terminal.test_boundary: the artifact workflow's own smoke job
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One assembly step inside the job that already stages the archive, proven by the smoke job that already extracts it.

title: Take the workflow profile and its presets out of the binary
description:
The binary compiles in no profile package and no workflow preset, so nothing in it names one project's workflow.

## Background

Two things carry this repository's workflow inside the binary. The whole package directory is compiled in, and three gate presets are derived from it: the preset names come from the packaged plan template's node gates, and each preset's shape is deserialized from a packaged gate contribution. By the criterion separating engine capability from a specific application, both are applications: a preset named for one project's review gate is a named instance, and the package is that project's whole workflow.

They are one removal, not two. Removing the package alone leaves the preset constructors reading gate definitions from nothing; removing the presets alone leaves a package compiled in for no consumer that needs it there. The compiled-in origin the applied-profile record can carry goes with them, and so does the last-resort resolution branch behind the two better answers that already exist.

The generated preset reference is part of the same change for a mechanical reason: it is a projection of the built-in presets with a conformance assertion comparing the committed copy against the projection, so it fails in any revision where the presets are gone and it is not regenerated. What the page then projects is the portable checker syntax it also carries.

Nothing this removes takes a capability away from a repository. A gate key resolves through the repository's own registry when no preset supplies it, and a preset never overwrote an authored gate, so the removal changes only which branch resolves the same names.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: No profile package is compiled into the binary, and the compile-time inclusion and the dependency that provided it are gone.
- [hard] REQ-02: The built-in gate presets are gone; a repository's own presets still load, and a template naming a gate no preset and no registry entry supplies reports that gate.
- [hard] REQ-03: The applied-profile origin naming a compiled-in package is gone, and resolution has no compiled-in last resort.
- [hard] REQ-04: The committed preset reference equals the projection of what remains, in the same revision.
- [hard] REQ-05: No production or test path resolves a compiled-in package.

## Notes

This repository's own gate registry needs no edit: all its workflow gate keys are hand-authored with repository-script checkers, and none was supplied by a preset.

planning.outcome: The binary compiles in no profile package and no workflow preset, and the generated preset reference matches what remains.

terminal.test_boundary: the crate's own suite over a binary carrying no package
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One indivisible removal whose every caller was retargeted by its predecessors, plus the projection that fails in the same revision if it is not regenerated with it.

title: State the engine-vocabulary boundary in the invariant
description:
The project invariant carries no sanctioned exception for a workflow bundle, and says which names are part of a mechanism, so the rule is decidable where a reviewer will test it.

## Background

The invariant says engine logic is domain-agnostic and then carves out one exception: the planning-bracket preset trio, retained as the single binary-shipped preset bundle. That carve-out is what the ruling removes, and once the binary carries no preset bundle the sentence describes something that no longer exists.

Deleting the sentence alone would leave the rule ambiguous at its hardest case. Three engine constants name bracket vocabulary — the default planning role, the default breakdown role, and the default container anchor — and each is an overridable default of a generic mechanism, resolved through the repository's own bindings when it declares them. A stricter reading would delete them and force every repository to declare bindings it currently inherits. The amended statement therefore says positively what stays: a name a mechanism resolves through declared bindings is part of the mechanism, while a declaration naming a particular gate, template, or node type is not.

Module documentation asserting that the binary ships the trio goes stale in the same change and is corrected with it.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The invariant registry entry carries no sanctioned exception for any workflow bundle.
- [hard] REQ-02: Its statement says that a specific workflow reaches a repository as a profile package, and that a name a mechanism resolves through declared bindings is part of the mechanism.
- [hard] REQ-03: The projection of the registry into the agent guidance file is regenerated from the registry rather than edited.
- [hard] REQ-04: No module documentation asserts that the binary ships a workflow preset bundle.
- [hard] REQ-05: The three template mechanism-parameter defaults remain, and the amended statement is what admits them.

## Notes

The charter decision recording the bracket workflow needs no amendment: it says the template instantiates the bracket and the gates gate it, and says nothing about where the gate definitions ship.

planning.outcome: The project invariant carries no sanctioned workflow exception and says which names are mechanism vocabulary.

terminal.test_boundary: repository validation over the registry in its projected form
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One registry statement is rewritten and its projection regenerated, with the module docs that repeat it corrected.

title: Stop naming the package a build input
description:
Editing a packaged live source no longer reports an installed binary as stale, because the package is no longer an input to the binary.

## Background

A path predicate decides whether a changed repository file can affect the production binary, and the stale-binary report refuses to trust a binary built before such a file changed. The package directory is one of its entries, and it was true: the whole directory was compiled in, so editing any of it changed the binary.

It stops being true the moment the package leaves the binary. Left in place, the entry reports every package edit as invalidating an installed binary that it cannot affect, and every gate run behind that report refuses until a rebuild that changes nothing has happened.

The predicate stays what it is: a pure path test in the layer that performs no input or output, evaluated against whatever repository the binary is validating. Only the set of paths it names changes.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The build-input path predicate no longer matches the package directory.
- [hard] REQ-02: A change to a file under the package directory does not report an installed binary as stale.
- [hard] REQ-03: A change to a crate source still does.
- [hard] REQ-04: The predicate remains a pure path test in a layer that performs no input or output.

## Notes

Every other entry stays: the workspace manifests, the lock files, the build script, the crate sources, and the hook scripts all still affect the binary.

planning.outcome: Editing a packaged live source no longer reports an installed binary as stale.

terminal.test_boundary: in-crate assertions over the build-input predicate
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One entry leaves a path list, with the assertions that describe the list following it.

title: Retire the embedded-package vocabulary
description:
The package type, the commands over it, and their help name a profile package rather than an embedded one, so no superseded name survives the cutover.

## Background

The names were accurate while a package could only be compiled in: the package type, its size bounds, the resolver, the enumerator, the application entry point, and the command help that offers to list the profiles embedded in this binary. None of them is accurate afterwards — a package is read from a repository location, and the binary embeds nothing.

Leaving them is the compatibility residue the cutover rule rejects, and the cost is not only tidiness: the help text is an adopter-facing statement of what the command does, and the agent-facing bridge is generated from the same command schema, so a stale name travels outward.

The rename is mechanical and belongs after the removal rather than before it, because before it the names still describe something that exists.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The package type, its bounds, and the profile command entry points carry names describing a profile package rather than a compiled-in one.
- [hard] REQ-02: The command help and the adopter-facing command reference describe reading a package from a repository location.
- [hard] REQ-03: The agent-facing bridge is regenerated from the changed command schema and its coverage still passes.
- [hard] REQ-04: No superseded name survives as an alias or re-export.

## Notes

This changes names and the text describing them; no behaviour changes with it.

planning.outcome: The package type, its commands, and their help name a profile package rather than an embedded one.

terminal.test_boundary: the generated command-schema contract suite
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One rename sweep over names that already have exactly one meaning, with the generated bridge following the schema.

footprint.uncertainty: Which generated bridge files change follows from how the renamed command help reaches the bridge schema.

title: Describe obtaining and applying a profile package
description:
The adopter-facing documentation describes a profile that arrives as a published package and is applied from a location inside the repository.

## Background

The profile reference tells an adopter that this release exposes one immutable profile embedded in the binary, and that applying it needs no Git repository, network access, or jit source checkout. Half of that stays true and half stops: the application is still offline and still needs no checkout, but the bytes now have to have been obtained, and the release is where they come from.

The planning-bracket how-to has the same shape of change. Its instructions still work — a hand-authored template still applies — but the gate definitions its bracket needs are no longer supplied by the binary, so the page has to state the two routes an adopter has: apply the profile, or declare the three gates in the repository's own registry, which is what the profile would have contributed anyway.

Each of these facts has one home. The release's asset list belongs with the release policy, the installation steps with the installation guide, and what a profile is and how it is applied with the profile reference; a page needing another's fact cites it rather than restating it.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The profile reference describes a package obtained from a release and applied from a location inside the repository, and states exactly what the offline promise still covers.
- [hard] REQ-02: The installation guide names the package asset among what a release carries.
- [hard] REQ-03: The planning-bracket how-to states both routes to the bracket's gates.
- [hard] REQ-04: No adopter-facing page describes a profile or a preset bundle carried inside the binary.
- [hard] REQ-05: Each fact has one home, and a page needing another page's fact cites it.

## Notes

The pages describe the surface as it is; a narrative of what it used to be belongs in the release notes.

planning.outcome: The adopter documentation describes a profile that arrives as a published package and is applied from a repository location.

terminal.test_boundary: the mechanical documentation checks over the adopter surface
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One sweep over the pages whose premise the cutover changed, each edited once for the same fact.

title: Inventory the binary's declarative configuration and sequence its removal
description:
Every site in the binary that carries declarative configuration is inventoried against the boundary in `@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-13`, and the removal of the whole set is sequenced with evidence, so it can be executed rather than debated.

## Background

`@/invariant/domain-agnostic` says the binary ships the mechanisms that interpret repository configuration and no instance of that configuration. `@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-13` fixes the boundary at its strictest reading: no type name, label namespace, item kind, documentation-area classification, or workflow rule reaches an adopter compiled into the executable that applies it, whether it names this repository or is generically opinionated. Only mechanism, and defaults for mechanism parameters (`@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-12`), remain.

A grep-assembled survey found eight sites and is not a basis for sequencing a change of this size. `crates/jit/src/profile/dogfood.rs` and the planning preset trio are already scoped for extraction by this epic. Beyond them the survey reached `SHIPPED_DOCUMENTATION_POLICY` (`crates/jit/src/config.rs:488`), which carries this repository's own development-area names and is what `jit init` scaffolds into an adopter's `[documentation]` table; `GENERATED_ARTIFACTS` (`crates/jit/src/generated_artifacts.rs:80`), which names this repository's generator scripts and documentation targets; the git hook scripts embedded by `crates/jit/src/commands/hooks.rs:7-8`; the configuration template `jit init` writes, declaring a type hierarchy, a namespace registry, and six item kinds; the seeded rules produced by `crates/jit/src/repository_state/default_rules.rs`; and the item-kind defaults at `crates/jit/src/domain/item.rs:55-64`. The survey is a starting point and is not authoritative: it did not distinguish a site that is one instance of a mechanism from a site that is the mechanism, and it did not look for sites that carry configuration without a constant to grep for.

Investigation `a62d444d` (`dev/active/a62d444d/findings.md`) established the mechanism, ordering, and consequences for the profile alone. Its §5.3 gives a five-step ordering whose steps 2 through 5 are unexecuted. This work extends that ordering rather than running beside it.

Six owner decisions bind this work and are not open: `@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-13` (the boundary), `D-14` (two packages, `jit-dogfood` declaring a dependency on `jit-default`), `D-15` (REQ-01's authority moves to the packaged declaration), `D-16` (both packages ride in the release archive), `D-17` (the registry-derived rules stay, `orphan-leaf` and `strategic-consistency` move), and `D-18` (this audit blocks fan-out).

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Every site in `crates/` carrying declarative configuration is inventoried with a file-and-line citation, each classified against D-13's boundary as an instance that leaves or a mechanism that stays, with the reason stated in the boundary's own terms. The inventory is established by reading the code rather than by extending the survey above, and a site the survey named but the reading rejects is reported as such.
- [hard] REQ-02: For each site that leaves, its destination is stated: `jit-default`, `jit-dogfood`, or deletion, with the reason. For each site that stays, what makes it a mechanism rather than an instance is stated in a form a reviewer can test.
- [hard] REQ-03: The composition mechanism D-14 requires is specified concretely — how a package declares its dependency on another, how application orders two packages, what happens when both declare the same key with different content, and how the provenance record and the applied-record wire shape represent a composed application. What already generalizes is separated from what must be built, each with a citation.
- [hard] REQ-04: `jit init`'s resulting shape is established: what a bare invocation writes, how `--profile <id> --from <path>` resolves and applies, what becomes of the present scaffold code path, and what an adopter does between unpacking a release archive and creating a first issue.
- [hard] REQ-05: The removal is sequenced as one ordering that extends `a62d444d` §5.3 rather than a second plan beside it. Every strict constraint is stated as an edge with the failure that makes it one, and every step that is indivisible is identified with the evidence for its indivisibility.
- [hard] REQ-06: The consequences for this epic's delivered work are stated per criterion, including REQ-01's retarget under D-15 and any other completed child whose result the removal invalidates, naming the issue and what specifically stops holding.
- [hard] REQ-07: The release-archive change D-16 requires is specified against the current release workflow and release-policy documentation, with its relationship to `@/charter/D-16` stated and any adopter-facing promise it breaks named.
- [hard] REQ-08: Costs with no route back are stated before execution: for each, the step at which the property disappears and the decision that must be taken at that step to preserve or deliberately drop it.
- [hard] REQ-09: Every claim about current behaviour carries a file-and-line citation, and no claim rests on inference where the code could be read.

## Non-goals

Implementing any of it. Editing the invariant registry, the charter, `.jit/` configuration, or any issue. Re-arguing the direction or any of the six binding decisions: evidence that a step is costly is a finding about cost and sequencing, not grounds to recommend against it.

## Notes

The report goes in this issue's artifact directory and is linked to the issue. `dev/active/a62d444d/findings.md` is the precedent for shape and depth, and its section-numbered citation form is reused so this epic's plan can address both reports the same way.

Fan-out on the widened scope blocks on this report (`@/issue/e204e63d/decision/D-18`). The extraction interior that `a62d444d` already sequenced is planned in the same pass, so the sequencing under REQ-05 must be usable as one manifest rather than two.

planning.outcome: Every site in the binary carrying declarative configuration is classified against the boundary and its removal sequenced.

terminal.test_boundary: the report's per-claim citation of the code it classifies
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One reading of one workspace against one boundary, producing the ordering the remaining removal is planned from.

warning_overrides.broad-quantifier: Completeness is the deliverable rather than an unbounded footprint: this exists because a partial survey is not a basis for sequencing a change of this size, and it produces one report and no code change.

title: The binary carries no workflow instance
description:
jit's own workflow profile and the presets derived from it are gone from the binary, riding in the release archive instead, and the invariant that governs the boundary says so without an exception.

## Background

The binary compiles in one project's whole workflow: the package directory, and three gate presets whose names and shapes are read out of it. The engine that interprets a workflow is capability; a particular workflow is not, and the invariant's carve-out for these three presets is the one place the code stands outside the rule that gates are declared in repository configuration rather than baked into the binary.

Removing them is bounded by two facts and one ordering. Nothing an adopter can do today stops working: a gate key resolves through the repository's own registry when no preset supplies it. Nothing this repository does stops working: its own bracket gates are hand-authored and it has never applied its own profile. And the package must ride in the release archive and be provably applicable from it before the compiled-in copy stops existing, so no release exists in which the profile is reachable only from a jit source checkout.

This is where the boundary starts rather than where it ends. The remaining embedded declarative configuration is inventoried and sequenced by the audit beside this work, and the resolver built here is the populated route that sequencing depends on.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The binary compiles in no profile package and no workflow preset.
- [hard] REQ-02: The release archive carries the assembled package beside the binaries, and the release smoke path applies the profile from it.
- [hard] REQ-03: The project invariant carries no sanctioned workflow exception and states which names belong to a mechanism.
- [hard] REQ-04: Nothing claims the package affects the binary: editing a packaged source does not report an installed binary as stale.
- [hard] REQ-05: No superseded embedded-package name survives, and the adopter-facing documentation describes obtaining and applying a published package.

## Notes

What the archive carries is the tree the derivation assembles, so this work consumes that artefact rather than producing one of its own.

planning.outcome: The workflow profile and its presets have left the binary, riding in the release archive instead.
